candidates: React hooks (including `useRef`, `useLandmark`, and any other custom hooks) must be declared unconditionally at the top level of a component function, before any early returns or conditional branches. If a hook call appears after an early return, move it above that return.

When refactoring the rendered element type of a component (e.g., changing `<div>` to `<nav>`, `<section>` to `<header>`, etc.), update every associated `useRef<T>` generic parameter to match the new element type (e.g., `useRef<HTMLDivElement>` → `useRef<HTMLElement>`), so the ref stays type-safe.

Prefer early-return guard clauses (`if (condition) return;`) over wrapping the primary logic in an `if`/`else` block. Early returns reduce nesting and preserve horizontal space for the meaningful code that follows.

Extract non-trivial inline logic (e.g., DOM traversal loops, complex derivations embedded inside effects or callbacks) into named helper functions at the module root rather than inlining them. This improves readability and makes the logic independently testable.

Auxiliary hooks that add ARIA or accessibility plumbing (e.g., `useLandmark`, `useId`) are implementation details in the context of their host component. Call them as compactly as readability allows—ideally on one or two lines—to avoid drawing disproportionate visual attention away from the component's primary logic.

When two subtrees are always rendered in a mutually exclusive, either/or fashion, express this with an `if`/`else` or a ternary (`condition ? <A /> : <B />`) rather than two separate standalone conditionals (`{condition && <A />}` followed by `{!condition && <B />}`). The former makes the mutual exclusivity self-evident to readers.

Before replacing a CSS-hide pattern (`display: none`, `visibility: hidden`, `hidden` attribute, or a wrapper that renders-but-conceals) with conditional mounting/unmounting, verify that the hidden component's internal state does not need to survive the hide/show cycle. Unmounting destroys state; CSS hiding preserves it.

When building a string array whose entries must match keys in a TypeScript interface or object literal (e.g., a `hardcodedShortcuts` or `fixedShortcuts` list used for filtering), verify the exact case-sensitive spelling of every entry. A casing mismatch compiles without error but silently fails to match at runtime, leaving the filtered logic broken.

When a UI region, label, shortcut, or interactive element is added or renamed, update all corresponding documentation prose—including section headings, paragraph descriptions, callout text, and link labels—to reflect the change accurately and completely.
